Local Well-posedness of the Coupled KdV-KdV Systems on ℝ\mathbb{R}

Xin Yang and Bing-Yu Zhang
Abstract

Inspired by the recent successful completion of the study of the well-posedness theory for the Cauchy problem of the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation

ut+u​ux+ux​x​x=0,u|t=0=u0u_{t}+uu_{x}+u_{xxx}=0,\quad\left.u\right|_{t=0}=u_{0}

in the space Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) (or Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T})), we study the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for a class of coupled KdV-KdV (cKdV) systems

{ut+a1​ux​x​x=c11​u​ux+c12​v​vx+d11​ux​v+d12​u​vx,vt+a2​vx​x​x=c21​u​ux+c22​v​vx+d21​ux​v+d22​u​vx,(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0)\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}+a_{1}u_{xxx}&=&c_{11}uu_{x}+c_{12}vv_{x}+d_{11}u_{x}v+d_{12}uv_{x},\\ v_{t}+a_{2}v_{xxx}&=&c_{21}uu_{x}+c_{22}vv_{x}+d_{21}u_{x}v+d_{22}uv_{x},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0})\end{array}\right.

in the space ℋs​(ℝ):=Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}):=H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}). Typical examples include the Gear-Grimshaw system, the Hirota-Satsuma system and the Majda-Biello system, to name a few. They usually serve as models to describe the interaction of two long waves with different dispersion relations.

In this paper we look for those values of s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R} for which the cKdV systems are well-posed in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}). Our findings enable us to provide a complete classification for the cKdV systems in terms of the analytical well-posedness in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) based on its coefficients aia_{i}, ci​jc_{ij} and di​jd_{ij} for i,j=1,2i,j=1,2. The key ingredients in the proofs are the bilinear estimates in both divergence and non-divergence forms under the Fourier restriction space norms. There are four types of the bilinear estimates that need to be investigated. Sharp results are established for all of them. In contrast to the lone critical index −34-\frac{3}{4} for the single KdV equation, the critical indexes for the cKdV systems are −1312-\frac{13}{12}, −34-\frac{3}{4}, 00 and 34\frac{3}{4}.

As a result, the cKdV systems are classified into four classes, each of which corresponds to a unique index s∗∈{−1312,−34, 0,34}s^{*}\in\{-\frac{13}{12},\,-\frac{3}{4},\,0,\,\frac{3}{4}\} such that any system in this class is locally analytically well-posed if s>s∗s>s^{*} while the bilinear estimate fails if s<s∗s<s^{*}.

1 Introduction

1.1 Problem to study

This paper studies the Cauchy problem of a class of coupled KdV-KdV systems posed on the whole line ℝ\mathbb{R} of the following general form,

{(utvt)+A1​(ux​x​xvx​x​x)+A2​(uxvx)=A3​(u​uxv​vx)+A4​(ux​vu​vx),x∈ℝ,t∈ℝ,(uv)|t=0=(u0v0),\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\begin{pmatrix}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{pmatrix}+A_{1}\begin{pmatrix}u_{xxx}\\ v_{xxx}\end{pmatrix}+A_{2}\begin{pmatrix}u_{x}\\ v_{x}\end{pmatrix}=A_{3}\begin{pmatrix}uu_{x}\\ vv_{x}\end{pmatrix}+A_{4}\begin{pmatrix}u_{x}v\\ uv_{x}\end{pmatrix},&x\in\mathbb{R},t\in\mathbb{R},\\ \left.\begin{pmatrix}u\\ v\end{pmatrix}\right|_{t=0}=\begin{pmatrix}u_{0}\\ v_{0}\end{pmatrix},\end{array}\right. (1.1)

where {Ai}1≤i≤4\{A_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq 4} are 2×22\times 2 real constant matrices, u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t), v=v⁡(x,t)v=v(x,t) are real-valued unknown functions of the two real variables xx and tt, and subscripts adorning uu and vv connote partial differentiations ∂t\partial_{t} or ∂x\partial_{x}. It is assumed that there exists an invertible real matrix MM such that

A1=M​(a100a2)​M−1,A_{1}=M\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}&0\\ 0&a_{2}\end{pmatrix}M^{-1},

with a1​a2≠0a_{1}a_{2}\neq 0. By regarding M−1​(uv)M^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}u\\ v\end{pmatrix} as the new unknown functions (still denoted by uu and vv), the system (1.1) can be rewritten in the following form,

{ut+a1​ux​x​x+b11​ux=−b12​vx+c11​u​ux+c12​v​vx+d11​ux​v+d12​u​vx,vt+a2​vx​x​x+b22​vx=−b21​ux+c21​u​ux+c22​v​vx+d21​ux​v+d22​u​vx,(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0).\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}+a_{1}u_{xxx}+b_{11}u_{x}&=&-b_{12}v_{x}+c_{11}uu_{x}+c_{12}vv_{x}+d_{11}u_{x}v+d_{12}uv_{x},\\ v_{t}+a_{2}v_{xxx}+b_{22}v_{x}&=&-b_{21}u_{x}+c_{21}uu_{x}+c_{22}vv_{x}+d_{21}u_{x}v+d_{22}uv_{x},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0}).\end{array}\right. (1.2)

This system is called in divergence form if d11=d12d_{11}=d_{12} and d21=d22d_{21}=d_{22}. Otherwise, it is called in non-divergence form.

Listed below are a few specializations of (1.1) appeared in the literature.

  • •

    Majda-Biello system:

    {ut+ux​x​x=−v​vx,vt+a2​vx​x​x=−(u​v)x,(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0),\left\{\begin{array}[]{rll}u_{t}+u_{xxx}&=&-vv_{x},\\ v_{t}+a_{2}v_{xxx}&=&-(uv)_{x},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0}),\end{array}\right. (1.3)

    where a2≠0a_{2}\neq 0. This system was proposed by Majda and Biello in [34] as a reduced asymptotic model to study the nonlinear resonant interactions of long wavelength equatorial Rossby waves and barotropic Rossby waves.

  • •

    Hirota-Satsuma system:

    {ut+a1​ux​x​x=−6​a1​u​ux+c12​v​vx,vt+vx​x​x=−3​u​vx,(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0),\left\{\begin{array}[]{rll}u_{t}+a_{1}u_{xxx}&=&-6a_{1}uu_{x}+c_{12}vv_{x},\\ v_{t}+v_{xxx}&=&-3uv_{x},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0}),\end{array}\right. (1.4)

    where a1≠0a_{1}\neq 0. This system was proposed by Hirota-Satsuma in [17] to describe the interaction of two long waves with different dispersion relations.

  • •

    Gear-Grimshaw system:

    {ut+ux​x​x+σ3​vx​x​x=−u​ux+σ1​v​vx+σ2​(u​v)x,ρ1​vt+ρ2​σ3​ux​x​x+vx​x​x+σ4​vx=ρ2​σ2​u​ux−v​vx+ρ2​σ1​(u​v)x,(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0),\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+\sigma_{3}v_{xxx}&=&-uu_{x}+\sigma_{1}vv_{x}+\sigma_{2}(uv)_{x},\\ \rho_{1}v_{t}+\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}u_{xxx}+v_{xxx}+\sigma_{4}v_{x}&=&\rho_{2}\sigma_{2}uu_{x}-vv_{x}+\rho_{2}\sigma_{1}(uv)_{x},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0}),\end{array}\right. (1.5)

    where σi∈ℝ⁡(1≤i≤4)\sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R}(1\leq i\leq 4) and ρ1,ρ2>0\rho_{1},\,\rho_{2}>0. This system is a special case of (1.1) by setting

    A1=(1σ3ρ2​σ3ρ11ρ1).A_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\sigma_{3}\\ \frac{\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}}{\rho_{1}}&\frac{1}{\rho_{1}}\end{pmatrix}. (1.6)

    Note that A1A_{1} in (1.6) is diagonalizable over ℝ\mathbb{R} for any σ3∈ℝ\sigma_{3}\in\mathbb{R} and ρ1,ρ2>0\rho_{1},\,\rho_{2}>0. Moreover, the eigenvalues of A1A_{1} are nonzero unless ρ2​σ32=1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}=1. So (1.5) can be reduced to the form (1.2) as long as ρ2​σ32≠1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}\neq 1. This system was derived by Gear-Grimshaw in [15] (also see [5] for the explanation about the physical context) as a model to describe the strong interaction of two-dimensional, weakly nonlinear, long, internal gravity waves propagating on neighboring pycnoclines in a stratified fluid, where the two waves correspond to different modes.

In this paper we study the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem (1.2) in the space

Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ)≜ℋs​(ℝ).H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\triangleq\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}).

The Cauchy problem (1.2) can be viewed as a special example of the following abstract Cauchy problem,

d​wd​t+L​w=N⁡(w),w⁡(0)=ϕ,\frac{dw}{dt}+Lw=N(w),\qquad w(0)=\phi, (1.7)

where LL is a linear operator, NN is a possibly time-dependent nonlinear operator and the initial datum ϕ\phi belongs to a Banach space 𝕏s\mathbb{X}_{s} with index s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}. The scale of Banach spaces 𝕏s\mathbb{X}_{s} has the property 𝕏s2⊂𝕏s1\mathbb{X}_{s_{2}}\subset\mathbb{X}_{s_{1}} if s1≤s2s_{1}\leq s_{2}. The well-posedness considered in this paper is understood in the following sense.

Definition 1.1.

The Cauchy problem (1.7) is said to be well-posed in the space 𝕏s\mathbb{X}_{s} if for any δ>0\delta>0 there is a T=T⁡(δ)>0T=T(\delta)>0 such that

  • (a)

    for any ϕ∈𝕏s\phi\in\mathbb{X}_{s} with ‖ϕ‖𝕏s≤δ\|\phi\|_{\mathbb{X}_{s}}\leq\delta, (1.7) admits exactly one solution ww in the space C⁡([0,T],𝕏s)C([0,T];\mathbb{X}_{s}) satisfying the auxiliary condition

    w∈𝕐sTw\in\mathbb{Y}^{T}_{s} (1.8)

    where 𝕐sT\mathbb{Y}^{T}_{s} is an auxiliary metric space;

  • (b)

    the solution ww depends continuously on its initial data ϕ\phi in the sense that the mapping ϕ→u\phi\to u is continuous from {ϕ:‖ϕ‖𝕏s≤δ}\{\phi:\|\phi\|_{\mathbb{X}_{s}}\leq\delta\} to C⁡([0,T],𝕏s)C([0,T];\mathbb{X}_{s}).

The well-posedness described by Definition 1.1 is local in character since the time TT depends on δ\delta. If TT can be specified independently of δ\delta in Definition 1.1, then (1.7) is said to be globally well-posed in the space 𝕏s\mathbb{X}_{s}. On the other hand, the Cauchy problem (1.7) is said to be (locally) uniformly well-posed, CkC^{k}-well-posed (k≥0k\geq 0), or analytically well-posed in the space 𝕏s\mathbb{X}_{s} if the corresponding solution map is (locally) uniform continuous, CkC^{k} or real analytic.

In this paper, we are looking for an answer to the following problem.

Problem: For what values of s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R} is the Cauchy problem (1.2) well-posed in the space ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R})?

1.2 Literature review

It is beneficial and instructive to the study of the Cauchy problem (1.2) by first reviewing the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem of the single KdV equation

ut+u​ux+ux​x​x=0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)u_{t}+\ uu_{x}+u_{xxx}=0,\qquad u(x,0)=u_{0}(x) (1.9)

posed either on the whole real line ℝ\mathbb{R} or on a periodic domain 𝕋\mathbb{T}. The study began in the late 1960s with the work of Sjöberg [44, 45] and has come to a happy end with the work of Killip and Visan[30]. Looking back, this study, which has lasted more than half a century, can be divided into four stages with four different major approaches developed in the process.

In Stage 1, (1.9) was most studied using traditionally PDE and functional analysis techniques. Sjöberg [44, 45] and Temam [49] (see [18, 51, 50, 42] and the references therein for some other works followed) obtained the existence and uniqueness of solutions of (1.9) on 𝕋\mathbb{T} in the space L∞​(0,T,H3​(𝕋))L^{\infty}(0,T;H^{3}(\mathbb{T})) (instead of in the space C⁡([0,T],H3​(𝕋))C([0,T];H^{3}(\mathbb{T}))), but without showing the continuity of the associated solution map. The first well-posedness result was due to Bona and Smith [6] who showed that (1.9) is (globally) well-posed in the space Hk​(ℝ)H^{k}(\mathbb{R}) or Hk​(𝕋)H^{k}(\mathbb{T}) for any integer k≥2k\geq 2 using a cleverly designed regularization scheme and classical energy estimate method. Then, (1.9) was shown by Bona and Scott [4] to be (globally) well-posed in the space Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) or Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for any real number s≥2s\geq 2 using Tartar’s nonlinear interpolation theory [48]. After this, as one of the applications of the semigroup theory, which is a powerful general theory dealing with various quasi-linear evolutionary PDEs, Kato[20, 21, 22, 23] showed that (1.9) is locally well-posed in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) or Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for any s>32s>\frac{3}{2}.

In Stage 2, as various smoothing properties of dispersive wave equations were discovered in 1980s (cf. [23, 12, 46, 25], Kenig, Ponce and Vega[24, 26, 28] were able to exploit the various dispersive smoothing properties of the linear KdV equation to show that (1.9) is locally well-posed in the space Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any s>34s>\frac{3}{4} by applying the contraction mapping principle in a carefully constructed Banach space, now known as the Kenig-Ponce-Vega (or KPV) space. As one of the key linear estimate fails when s<34s<\frac{3}{4}, one can only show that (1.9) is well-posed in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>34s>\frac{3}{4} using this approach.

In Stage 3, Bourgain[8] introduced the Fourier restriction spaces Xs,bX_{s,b} and showed that the Cauchy problem (1.9) is well-posed in both spaces Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) and Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for any s≥0s\geq 0 by using the contraction mapping principle in Xs,bX_{s,b}. Then Kenig, Ponce and Vega[29] showed that (1.9) is locally well-posed in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} and in Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for any s≥−12s\geq-\frac{1}{2}. The local well-posedness of (1.9) in the space H−34​(ℝ)H^{-\frac{3}{4}}(\mathbb{R}) was established by Christ, Colliander and Tao[10]. The thresholds −34-\frac{3}{4} for Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) and −12-\frac{1}{2} for Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) are sharp if one requires the solution map to be uniformly continuous, see [10]. Moreover, (1.9) has been shown to be globally well-posed in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥−34s\geq-\frac{3}{4} and in Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for s≥−12s\geq-\frac{1}{2} (see [11, 16, 31]).

In Stage 4, Kappeler and Topalov [19] proved that (1.9) is globally well-posed in the space Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for any s≥−1s\geq-1 by developing a new approach based on the inverse scattering method. Recently, Killip and Visan [30] showed that (1.9) is globally well-posed in the space H−1​(ℝ)H^{-1}(\mathbb{R}) by introducing a new method of general applicability for the study of low-regularity well-posedness for integrable PDE. As it has already been shown by Molinet [35, 36] that (1.9) is ill-posed in both Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) and Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for any s<−1s<-1, the study of the well-posedness of (1.9) has drawn a satisfactory conclusion.

There is a difference between the well-posdenss presented in Stages 1 and 4 and those presented in Stages 2 and 3. For the well-posedness obtained in Stage 1 and 4, the solution of (1.9) depends only continuously on its initial value. By contrast, for the well-posedness established in Stage 2 and 3, one can show the solution of (1.9) depends on its initial value analytically (cf. [54, 53, 52]). Thus the Cauchy problem (1.9) is analytically well-posed in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥−34s\geq-\frac{3}{4} and in Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for s≥−12s\geq-\frac{1}{2}, but is only continuously well-posed in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for −1≤s<−34-1\leq s<-\frac{3}{4} and in Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}) for −1≤s<−12-1\leq s<-\frac{1}{2} .

Naturally, following the advances of the study of the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem (1.9) for the single KdV equation, there have been many works on the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem (1.2) for the coupled KdV-KdV systems. Here we provide a brief summary of the previous results on ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}). As a convenience of the notation, LWP and GWP will stand for local well-posedness and global well-posedness.

  • •

    Majda-Biello system (1.3).

    • –

      If a2=1a_{2}=1, the LWP in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} follows immeidately from the single KdV theory. The GWP in ℋs\mathcal{H}^{s} for any s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} was justified by Oh[37] via the I-method.

    • –

      If a2∈(0,4)∖{1}a_{2}\in(0,4)\setminus\{1\}, Oh[38] proved that (1.3) is locally well-posed in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥0s\geq 0 and ill-posed when s<0s<0 if the solution map is required to be C2C^{2}. The key ingredient in the proof for the LWP is the bilinear estimate under the Fourier restriction norm. Due to the L2L^{2} conservation law of (1.3), its GWP in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥0s\geq 0 automatically holds.

  • •

    Hirota-Satsuma system (1.4).

    • –

      Alvarez-Carvajal[1] proved the LWP for (1.4) in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>34s>\frac{3}{4} via the method in [26].

    • –

      Feng[14] considered a slightly general system:

      {ut+a1​ux​x​x=−6​a1​u​ux+c12​v​vx,vt+vx​x​x=c22​v​vx+d22​u​vx,(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0).\left\{\begin{array}[]{rll}u_{t}+a_{1}u_{xxx}&=&-6a_{1}uu_{x}+c_{12}vv_{x},\\ v_{t}+v_{xxx}&=&c_{22}vv_{x}+d_{22}uv_{x},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0}).\end{array}\right. (1.10)

      When c22=0c_{22}=0 and d22=−3d_{22}=-3, (1.10) reduces to the original Hirota-Satusma system (1.4). Feng proved the LWP of (1.10) in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥1s\geq 1 under the assumption that a1≠1a_{1}\neq 1 and c12​d22<0c_{12}d_{22}<0. The GWP was also shown by the further restriction that 0<a1<10<a_{1}<1.

  • •

    Gear-Grimshaw system (1.5).

    • –

      Assume σ4=0\sigma_{4}=0 and ρ2​σ32≠1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}\neq 1. Bona-Ponce-Saut-Tom[5] proved the LWP of (1.5) in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥1s\geq 1. They also showed the GWP of (1.5) in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥1s\geq 1 under further assumption that ρ2​σ32<1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}<1.

    • –

      Later, further LWP and GWP results were proven by Ash-Cohen-Wang[2], Linares-Panthee[33] and Saut-Tzvetkov[43], where the best LWP result is proven in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4}. However, their argument essentially requires the matrix A1A_{1} in (1.6) to be similar to the identity matrix, which means σ3=0\sigma_{3}=0 and ρ1=1\rho_{1}=1. Equivalently, if considering the diagonalized system (1.2), their results are only valid under the assumption that a1=a2a_{1}=a_{2} (see Remark 1.2 in [38] and Remark 3.1 in [1] for more detailed explanations).

  • •

    General coupled KdV-KdV systems

    • –

      Alvarez-Carvajal[1] considered the diagonalized system (1.2) where (bi​j)=0(b_{ij})=0, d11=d12d_{11}=d_{12} and d21=d22d_{21}=d_{22}, i.e.,

      {ut+a1​ux​x​x=c11​u​ux+c12​v​vx+d11​(u​v)x,vt+a2​vx​x​x=c21​u​ux+c22​v​vx+d22​(u​v)x,(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0).\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}+a_{1}u_{xxx}&=&c_{11}uu_{x}+c_{12}vv_{x}+d_{11}(uv)_{x},\\ v_{t}+a_{2}v_{xxx}&=&c_{21}uu_{x}+c_{22}vv_{x}+d_{22}(uv)_{x},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0}).\end{array}\right. (1.11)

      They proved that (1.11) is locally well-posed in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} if a1=−a2≠0a_{1}=-a_{2}\neq 0. The key tool in their proof is the bilinear estimate under the Fourier restriction norm. The question whether (1.11) is well-posed in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) when |a1|≠|a2||a_{1}|\neq|a_{2}| is left open in [1]. On the other hand, Alvarez-Carvaja’s result in [1] actually does not apply to the Gear-Grimshaw system (1.5) since a1=−a2>0a_{1}=-a_{2}>0 implies ρ1=−1\rho_{1}=-1 which is against the assumption ρ1>0\rho_{1}>0.

1.3 Main results on well-posedness

As we have seen from the literature review, the dispersion coefficients a1a_{1} and a2a_{2}, and other coefficients (bi​j)(b_{ij}), (ci​j)(c_{ij}) and (di​j)(d_{ij}), in the systems (1.2) have significant impact on the well-posedness results. The following theorem is the main finding we have obtained so far.

Theorem 1.2.

Let a1,a2∈ℝ∖{0}a_{1},\,a_{2}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} and denote r=a2a1r=\dfrac{a_{2}}{a_{1}}. Then (1.2) is locally analytically well-posed in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any case in Table 1.

The well-posedness results presented in Theorem 1.2 are sharp in the sense that the key bilinear estimates used in their proofs are sharp (up to the endpoints), see Theorem 3.3–3.6.

As applications, we apply Theorem 1.2 to a few specializations of (1.2). First, we consider a special class of (1.2) of the following form

{ut+a1​ux​x​x=d1​(u​v)x,vt+a2​vx​x​x=d2​(u​v)x,(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0).\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}+a_{1}u_{xxx}&=&d_{1}(uv)_{x},\\ v_{t}+a_{2}v_{xxx}&=&d_{2}(uv)_{x},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0}).\end{array}\right. (1.12)
Theorem 1.3.

If a1​a2<0a_{1}a_{2}<0, then the system (1.12) is locally analytically well-posed in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥−1312s\geq-\frac{13}{12}.

The above theorem is surprising since even the Cauchy problem (1.9) of the single KdV equation is ill-posed in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any s<−1s<-1.

Theorem 1.4.

The Majda-Biello system (1.3), where a2≠0a_{2}\neq 0, is locally (resp. globally) analytically well-posed in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any case in Table 7 (resp. Table 7).

Remark: in Theorem 1.4, Case (1) and (2) in Table 7 and 7 have been known earlier in Oh[38, 37].

Theorem 1.5.

The Hirota-Satsuma systems (1.4), where a1≠0a_{1}\neq 0, is locally (resp. globally) analytically well-posed in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any case in Table 13 (resp. Table 13).

We finally turn to the Gear-Grimshaw system (1.5) and introduce the condition (1.13) for convenience.

ρ2​σ32≤925andρ12+25​ρ2​σ32−174​ρ1+1=0.\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}\leq\frac{9}{25}\quad\text{and}\quad\rho_{1}^{2}+\frac{25\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}-17}{4}\rho_{1}+1=0. (1.13)
Theorem 1.6.

The Gear-Grimshaw system (1.5), where ρ1,ρ2>0\rho_{1},\,\rho_{2}>0, is locally (resp. globally) analytically well-posed in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any case in Table 19 (resp. Table 19).

It should be pointed out that Case (1) in Table 19 is trivial since it directly follows from the proof of the single KdV case.

1.4 Remarks

A few remarks are now in order.

Remark 1.7.

While the results presented in Section 1.3 provides a rather thorough description of the analytically well-posedness in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for the systems (1.2), the study of the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem of (1.2) in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) is far from over in comparison to the study of the KdV equation (1.9). We list below a few problems among many to be investigated.

  • •

    Question 1.1: For the locally analytically well-posedness results of (1.2) listed in Table 1, it requires s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} in Cases (1), (2), (5) and (8). Can those results be strengthened to include s=−34s=-\frac{3}{4}?

  • •

    Question 1.2: The locally analytically well-posedness results of the systems (1.2) listed in Table 1 are sharp in the sense that the needed bilinear estimates, a key ingredient in the proofs, fail if ss is less than the corresponding critical index s∗s^{*}. Is the Cauchy problem of (1.2) analytically ill-posed in the space ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for any ss which is less than the corresponding critical index s∗s^{*}?

  • •

    Question 1.3: Can those locally analytically well-posedness results of the systems (1.2) listed in Table 1 be strengthened to be globally analytically well-posed results?

Remark 1.8.

As hinted by the study of the single KdV equation, the answers to both Question 1.1 and Question 1.2 will most likely be positive. For Question 1.1, some more subtly modified Bourgain spaces may need to be constructed, see e.g. [16, 31]. For Question1.2, some counter examples are needed to show that the solution map fails to be smooth if ss is less than the corresponding critical index s∗s^{*}. We leave this study to future works since the current paper is already long.

Remark 1.9.

For Question 1.3, as long as one can establish a priori global ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) estimates for solutions of the system (1.2), the GWP of (1.2) in ℋs​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}^{s}(\mathbb{R}) follows from the corresponding LWP result. In particular, when there are conserved energy at certain regularity level, the corresponding GWP can be easily verified. For example, we also include some GWP results in Theorem 1.4–1.6. But if the regularity considered in the well-posedness problem is lower than the level provided by the available conserved energy, one may need to apply other methods, such as the I-method [11], to establish the GWP.

Remark 1.10.

The single KdV equation has also been intensively studied from control point of views for its controllability and stabilizability (the interested readers are referred to [41, 55, 39, 9, 13, 56, 40, 32] and the references therein for an overview of this subject). Various tools developed in the study of the welll-posedness of the single KdV equation have played important roles in studying control theory of the KdV equation. By contrast, there are few studies of the systems (1.2) from control points of view. We expect the results and the tools obtained and developed in the study of the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem of (1.2) will stimulate and play important roles in further studies of the control theory for the coupled KdV-KdV systems.

1.5 Organization

The remaining of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, some linear estimates are recalled or proved as a preparation. In Section 3, we present our main results on the bilinear estimates which are the key ingredients in the proof of the main well-posedness result: Theorem 1.2. The proofs of these bilinear estimates will be postponed to Sections 5 and 6. In Section 4, we prove Theorem 1.2, and its consequences, Theorem 1.3–1.6. Section 5 is devoted to establish the various bilinear estimates, Theorem 3.3 and 3.5, presented in Section 3. Finally, Section 6 is dedicated to justify Theorem 3.4 and 3.6 which exposit the sharpness of the various bilinear estimates.

3 Main results on bilinear estimates

Our main well-posedness results in Theorem 1.2 will be proved using the same approach as that developed by Bourgain [7, 8], Kenig-Ponce -Vega [29] in establishing analytical well-posedness of the Cauchy problem of (1.9) in the space Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4}. The key ingredient in the approach is the bilinear estimate under the Fourier restriction space (also called Bourgain space). Let us first introduce the definition of this space. For any α,β∈ℝ\alpha,\,\beta\in\mathbb{R} with α≠0\alpha\neq 0, denote the polymomial ϕα,β\phi^{\alpha,\beta} as

ϕα,β​(ξ)=α​ξ3−β​ξ.\phi^{\alpha,\beta}(\xi)=\alpha\xi^{3}-\beta\xi. (3.1)

For convenience, ϕα,0\phi^{\alpha,0} will be denoted as ϕα\phi^{\alpha}. Then the Fourier restriction space is defined as follows.

Definition 3.1.

For any α,β,s,b∈ℝ\alpha,\,\beta,\,s,\,b\in\mathbb{R} with α≠0\alpha\neq 0, the Fourier restriction space Xs,bα,βX^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b} is defined to be the completion of the Schwartz space 𝒮⁡(ℝ2)\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) with respect to the norm

‖w‖Xs,bα,β=‖⟨ξ⟩s​⟨τ−ϕα,β​(ξ)⟩b​w^​(ξ,τ)‖L2​(d​ξ​d​τ),\|w\|_{X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b}}=\|\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\tau-\phi^{\alpha,\beta}(\xi)\rangle^{b}\widehat{w}(\xi,\tau)\|_{L^{2}(d\xi d\tau)}, (3.2)

where ⟨⋅⟩=1+|⋅|\langle\cdot\rangle=1+|\cdot|, ϕα,β\phi^{\alpha,\beta} is given by (3.1), and w^\widehat{w} refers to the space-time Fourier transform of ww. Moreover, Xs,bα,0X^{\alpha,0}_{s,b} is simply denoted as Xs,bαX^{\alpha}_{s,b}. On the other hand, for any T>0T>0, Xs,bα,β​([0,T])X^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b}([0,T]) denotes the restriction of Xs,bα,βX^{\alpha,\beta}_{s,b} on the domain ℝ×[0,T]\mathbb{R}\times[0,T] which is a Banach space when equipped with the usual quotient norm.

The bilinear estimate which was first considered by Bourgain[8] is the following one:

‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Xs,b−11≤C​‖w1‖Xs,b1​‖w2‖Xs,b1,∀w1,w2.\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{X^{1}_{s,b-1}}\leq C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{1}_{s,b}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{1}_{s,b}},\quad\forall w_{1},w_{2}. (3.3)

Bourgain proved (3.3) for s=0s=0 and b=12b=\frac{1}{2} while the following lemma is due to Kening, Ponce and Vega.

Lemma 3.2 (Kenig-Ponce-Vega [29]).

The bilinear estimate (3.3) holds for any s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} and b∈(12,b0​(s))b\in\big(\frac{1}{2},b_{0}(s)\big) with some b0​(s)>12b_{0}(s)>\frac{1}{2}, but fails for any b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} if s<−34s<-\frac{3}{4}.

In order to deal with the general KdV-KdV systems (1.2), four types of bilinear estimates need to be investigated. In (3.4)-(3.7), (D)(D) represents divergence form and (ND) refers to non-divergence form.

(D1):∥∂x(w1w2)∥Xs,b−1α2,β2≤C∥w1∥Xs,bα1,β1∥w2∥Xs,bα1,β1,∀w1,w2.\displaystyle\text{(D1):}\qquad\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{X^{\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}}_{s,b-1}}\leq C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b}},\quad\forall\,w_{1},w_{2}. (3.4)
(D2):∥∂x(w1w2)∥Xs,b−1α1,β1≤C∥w1∥Xs,bα1,β1∥w2∥Xs,bα2,β2,∀w1,w2.\displaystyle\text{(D2):}\qquad\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b-1}}\leq C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}}_{s,b}},\quad\forall\,w_{1},w_{2}. (3.5)

and

(ND1):∥(∂xw1)w2∥Xs,b−1α1,β1≤C∥w1∥Xs,bα1,β1∥w2∥Xs,bα2,β2,∀w1,w2.\displaystyle\text{(ND1):}\qquad\|(\partial_{x}w_{1})w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b-1}}\leq C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}}_{s,b}},\quad\forall\,w_{1},w_{2}. (3.6)
(ND2):∥w1(∂xw2)∥Xs,b−1α1,β1≤C∥w1∥Xs,bα1,β1∥w2∥Xs,bα2,β2,∀w1,w2.\displaystyle\text{(ND2):}\qquad\|w_{1}(\partial_{x}w_{2})\|_{X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b-1}}\leq C\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}}_{s,b}},\quad\forall\,w_{1},w_{2}. (3.7)

Here, (α1,β1)(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}) (or OPEN(α2,β2))(\alpha_{2},\beta_{2})\big) stands for (a1,b11)(a_{1},b_{11}) or (a2,b22)(a_{2},b_{22}). (D1) is used to deal with the square terms u​uxuu_{x} and v​vxvv_{x} in (1.2). (D2) is responsible for the mixed divergence term (u​v)x(uv)_{x} when d11=d12d_{11}=d_{12} or d21=d22d_{21}=d_{22} in (1.2). (ND1) and (ND2) are applied to treat the mixed non-divergence terms ux​vu_{x}v and u​vxuv_{x} when d11≠d12d_{11}\neq d_{12} or d21≠d22d_{21}\neq d_{22}. On the other hand, (D1) is different from (D2) since w1w_{1} and w2w_{2} live in the same space Xs,bα1,β1X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b} for (D1) but in different spaces for (D2). (ND1) is also slightly different from (ND2). Nevertheless, due to the relation (w1​w2)x=(∂xw1)​w2+w1​(∂xw2)(w_{1}w_{2})_{x}=(\partial_{x}w_{1})w_{2}+w_{1}(\partial_{x}w_{2}), any results for (ND2) can be automatically obtained once the corresponding results are known for (D2) and (ND1). The main challenges of studying the bilinear estimates (3.4)– (3.7) come from either the distinct dispersion coefficients α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} or the non-divergence form.

Theorem 3.3.

Let α1​α2<0\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}<0. Assume ss and bb satisfy one of the following conditions.

  1. (1)

    −1312≤s≤−1-\frac{13}{12}\leq s\leq-1 and 14−s3≤b≤43+2​s3\frac{1}{4}-\frac{s}{3}\leq b\leq\frac{4}{3}+\frac{2s}{3};

  2. (2)

    −1<s<−34-1<s<-\frac{3}{4} and 14−s3≤b≤1+s3\frac{1}{4}-\frac{s}{3}\leq b\leq 1+\frac{s}{3};

  3. (3)

    s≥−34s\geq-\frac{3}{4} and 12<b<34\frac{1}{2}<b<\frac{3}{4}.

Then there exist ϵ=ϵ⁡(α1,α2)\epsilon=\epsilon(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}) and C=C⁡(α1,α2,s,b)C=C(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},s,b) such that for any |β2−β1|≤ϵ|\beta_{2}-\beta_{1}|\leq\epsilon, (3.5) holds.

For the convenience of the readers, we draw a picture of the range of ss and bb when s<−34s<-\frac{3}{4}, see Figure 1. This range is sharp due to Theorem 3.4.

Theorem 3.4.

Let α1​α2<0\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}<0 and β1=β2=β\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta. Assume ss and bb satisfy one of the following conditions.

  1. (1)

    s<−1312s<-\frac{13}{12} and b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R};

  2. (2)

    −1312≤s≤−1-\frac{13}{12}\leq s\leq-1 and b∉[14−s3,43+2​s3]b\notin[\frac{1}{4}-\frac{s}{3},\,\frac{4}{3}+\frac{2s}{3}];

  3. (3)

    −1<s<−34-1<s<-\frac{3}{4} and b∉[14−s3, 1+s3]b\notin[\frac{1}{4}-\frac{s}{3},\,1+\frac{s}{3}].

Then there does not exist any constant C=C⁡(α1,α2,β,s,b)C=C(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta,s,b) such that (3.5) holds.

The results presented in Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 3.4 together are surprising in comparison to the previous results on the bilinear estimate.

  • •

    First, in the case of the single KdV equation (1.9), the critical index for the corresponding bilinear estimate (3.3) is −34-\frac{3}{4}. However, when α1​α2<0\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}<0, the critical index of the bilinear estiamte (3.5) of type (D2) can be as low as −1312-\frac{13}{12}.

  • •

    Secondly, for the previous biliear estimates, bb is usually required to be close to 12\frac{1}{2} as ss approaches to the critical threshold. However, for the bilinear estimate (3.5) with α1​α2<0\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}<0 and −1312≤s<−34-\frac{13}{12}\leq s<-\frac{3}{4}, bb needs to be away from 12\frac{1}{2}. In particular, when s=−1312s=-\frac{13}{12}, bb needs to be exactly 1118\frac{11}{18}.

Theorem 3.5.

Let α1,α2∈ℝ∖{0}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} and denote r=α2α1r=\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{1}}. Assume rr, ss and the bilinear estimate type belong to any case in Table 20. Then there exist b0=b0​(s)>12b_{0}=b_{0}(s)>\frac{1}{2} and ϵ=ϵ⁡(α1,α2)\epsilon=\epsilon(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}) such that for any 12<b≤b0\frac{1}{2}<b\leq b_{0} and for any |β2−β1|≤ϵ|\beta_{2}-\beta_{1}|\leq\epsilon, the bilinear estimate holds with some constant C=C⁡(α1,α2,s,b)C=C(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},s,b).

The indexes in Table 20 are also sharp.

Theorem 3.6.

Let α1,α2∈ℝ∖{0}\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} and denote r=α2α1r=\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{1}}. Let β1=β2=β\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta. Assume rr, ss and the bilinear estimate type belong to any case in Table 21. Then for any b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R}, there does not exist a constant C=C⁡(α1,α2,β,s,b)C=C(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta,s,b) such that the bilinear estimate holds.

There are several things worth mentioning about Theorem 3.5 and 3.6. First, when r<0r<0, the critical index for Type (D1) is −34-\frac{3}{4} which is much larger than that for Type (D2), see Theorem 3.3. Secondly, when r=14r=\frac{1}{4}, the critical index is 34\frac{3}{4} which is much larger than other cases for r≠14r\neq\frac{1}{4}. Thirdly, when r=1r=1, the critical index is −34-\frac{3}{4} for the divergence forms but is 00 for the non-divergence forms.

Remark 3.7.

Some results in Theorem 3.5 and 3.6 have already been known (or can be proven similarly) in the previous literatures. More specifically, in Table 20 and 21, when r=1r=1, Type (D1) and (D2) have been established in [29]; when r>14r>\frac{1}{4} but r≠1r\neq 1, Type (D1) and (D2) have been justified in [38], and Type (ND1) and (ND2) can be proven similarly. But note that the notations in [38] are slightly different from here. Actually, the roles of α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} are interchanged there. In Table 8 with r=−1r=-1, Type (D1) has appeared in [1].

The proofs of Theorem 3.3–3.6 are very technical and tedious, so we postpone them to Section 5 and 6.

4.2 Proofs of Theorem 1.3 – Theorem 1.6

Theorem 1.3 follows directly from Case (1) in Theorem 1.2.

For the Majda-Biello system (1.3), it is a special case of (1.2) with the coefficients

a1=1;(bi​j)=0;c11=c21=c22=0,c12=−1;d11=d12=0,d21=d22=−1.\begin{split}&a_{1}=1;\quad(b_{ij})=0;\quad c_{11}=c_{21}=c_{22}=0,\,c_{12}=-1;\\ &d_{11}=d_{12}=0,\,d_{21}=d_{22}=-1.\end{split} (4.18)

So the LWP results in Theorem 1.4 follow directly from Theorem 1.2. Then according to these LWP results and the conserved energies (4.19), the GWP results in Theorem 1.4 are established (except when a2=1a_{2}=1 for which case the GWP was proved for any s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} by Oh[37] via the I-method).

E1​(u,v)=∫u2+v2​dx,E2​(u,v)=∫ux2+a2​vx2−u​v2​dx.\begin{split}E_{1}(u,v)&=\int u^{2}+v^{2}\,dx,\\ E_{2}(u,v)&=\int u_{x}^{2}+a_{2}v_{x}^{2}-uv^{2}\,dx.\end{split} (4.19)

For the Hirota-Satsuma system (1.4), it is a special case of (1.2) with the coefficients

a2=1;(bi​j)=0;c11=−6a1,c21=c22=0;d11=d12=d21=0,d22=−3.\begin{split}&a_{2}=1;\quad(b_{ij})=0;\quad c_{11}=-6a_{1},\,c_{21}=c_{22}=0;\\ &d_{11}=d_{12}=d_{21}=0,\,d_{22}=-3.\end{split} (4.20)

So the LWP results in Theorem 1.5 follow directly from Theorem 1.2. Then according to these LWP results and the conserved energies (4.21), the GWP results in Theorem 1.5 are established.

E1​(u,v)=∫u2+c123​v2​dx,E2​(u,v)=∫(1−a1)​ux2+c12​vx2−2​(1−a1)​u3−c12​u​v2​dx.\begin{split}E_{1}(u,v)&=\int u^{2}+\frac{c_{12}}{3}v^{2}\,dx,\\ E_{2}(u,v)&=\int(1-a_{1})u_{x}^{2}+c_{12}v_{x}^{2}-2(1-a_{1})u^{3}-c_{12}uv^{2}\,dx.\end{split} (4.21)

For the Gear-Grimshaw system (1.5), we first write it into the vector form:

{(utvt)+A1​(ux​x​xvx​x​x)+A2​(uxvx)=A3​(u​uxv​vx)+A4​(ux​vu​vx),(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0),\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}\begin{pmatrix}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{pmatrix}+A_{1}\begin{pmatrix}u_{xxx}\\ v_{xxx}\end{pmatrix}+A_{2}\begin{pmatrix}u_{x}\\ v_{x}\end{pmatrix}&=&A_{3}\begin{pmatrix}uu_{x}\\ vv_{x}\end{pmatrix}+A_{4}\begin{pmatrix}u_{x}v\\ uv_{x}\end{pmatrix},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0}),\end{array}\right. (4.22)

where

A1=(1σ3ρ2​σ3ρ11ρ1),A2=(000σ4ρ1),A3=(−1σ1ρ2​σ2ρ1−1ρ1),A4=(σ2σ2ρ2​σ1ρ1ρ2​σ1ρ1).A_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\sigma_{3}\\ \frac{\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}}{\rho_{1}}&\frac{1}{\rho_{1}}\end{pmatrix},\quad A_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&\frac{\sigma_{4}}{\rho_{1}}\end{pmatrix},\quad A_{3}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&\sigma_{1}\\ \frac{\rho_{2}\sigma_{2}}{\rho_{1}}&-\frac{1}{\rho_{1}}\end{pmatrix},\quad A_{4}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{2}&\sigma_{2}\\ \frac{\rho_{2}\sigma_{1}}{\rho_{1}}&\frac{\rho_{2}\sigma_{1}}{\rho_{1}}\end{pmatrix}.

When ρ2​σ32≠1\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}\neq 1, A1A_{1} has two nonzero eigenvalues λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2}:

λ1=ρ1+12​ρ1+(ρ1−1)2+4​ρ1​ρ2​σ322​ρ1,λ2=ρ1+12​ρ1−(ρ1−1)2+4​ρ1​ρ2​σ322​ρ1.\lambda_{1}=\frac{\rho_{1}+1}{2\rho_{1}}+\frac{\sqrt{(\rho_{1}-1)^{2}+4\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}}}{2\rho_{1}},\qquad\lambda_{2}=\frac{\rho_{1}+1}{2\rho_{1}}-\frac{\sqrt{(\rho_{1}-1)^{2}+4\rho_{1}\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}}}{2\rho_{1}}. (4.23)

So there exists an invertible real-valued matrix MM such that A1=M​(λ1λ2)​M−1A_{1}=M\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{1}&\\ &\lambda_{2}\end{pmatrix}M^{-1}. By regarding M−1​(uv)M^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}u\\ v\end{pmatrix} as the new unknown functions (still denoted by uu and vv), (4.22) can be rewritten as

{(utvt)+(λ1λ2)​(ux​x​xvx​x​x)+B​(uxvx)=C​(u​uxv​vx)+D​(ux​vu​vx),(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0),\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}\begin{pmatrix}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_{1}&\\ &\lambda_{2}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}u_{xxx}\\ v_{xxx}\end{pmatrix}+B\begin{pmatrix}u_{x}\\ v_{x}\end{pmatrix}&=&C\begin{pmatrix}uu_{x}\\ vv_{x}\end{pmatrix}+D\begin{pmatrix}u_{x}v\\ uv_{x}\end{pmatrix},\\ \left.(u,v)\right|_{t=0}&=&(u_{0},v_{0}),\end{array}\right. (4.24)

where d11=d12d_{11}=d_{12}, d21=d22d_{21}=d_{22}. In addition, B=(0000)B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix} if σ4=0\sigma_{4}=0. Define

r=λ2λ1.r=\frac{\lambda_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}. (4.25)

Then it follows from (4.23) that r<1r<1. Moreover, since both ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} are positive numbers, we have r<0⟺ρ2​σ32>1r<0\Longleftrightarrow\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}>1. Moreover, r=14r=\frac{1}{4} if and only if (1.13) holds, that is

ρ2​σ32≤925andρ12+25​ρ2​σ32−174​ρ1+1=0.\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}\leq\frac{9}{25}\quad\text{and}\quad\rho_{1}^{2}+\frac{25\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}^{2}-17}{4}\rho_{1}+1=0.

Based on the above observations, the LWP results in Theorem 1.6 follow from Theorem 1.2. Then according to these LWP results and the conserved energies (4.26), the GWP results in Theorem 1.6 are established.

E1​(u,v)=∫ρ2​u2+ρ1​v2​dx,E2​(u,v)=∫ρ2​ux2+vx2+2​ρ2​σ3​ux​vx−ρ23​u3+ρ2​σ2​u2​v+ρ2​σ1​u​v2−13​v3−σ4​v2.\begin{split}E_{1}(u,v)&=\int\rho_{2}u^{2}+\rho_{1}v^{2}\,dx,\\ E_{2}(u,v)&=\int\rho_{2}u_{x}^{2}+v_{x}^{2}+2\rho_{2}\sigma_{3}u_{x}v_{x}-\frac{\rho_{2}}{3}u^{3}+\rho_{2}\sigma_{2}u^{2}v+\rho_{2}\sigma_{1}uv^{2}-\frac{1}{3}v^{3}-\sigma_{4}v^{2}.\end{split} (4.26)

5 Proofs of the bilinear estimates

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 3.5.

5.1 Idea of the proofs

The main idea of treating the bilinear estimates of different types are similar, and is thus explained only for the following divergence form with βi=0​(i=1,2,3)\beta_{i}=0\,(i=1,2,3).

‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Xs,b−1α3≲‖w1‖Xs,bα1​‖w2‖Xs,bα2,∀w1,w2.\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{X^{\alpha_{3}}_{s,b-1}}\lesssim\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha_{1}}_{s,b}}\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha_{2}}_{s,b}},\quad\forall\,w_{1},w_{2}. (5.1)

By duality and Plancherel identity, (5.1) is equivalent to (see e.g. [47])

|∫∑i=13ξi=0∫∑i=13τi=0ξ3​⟨ξ3⟩s​∏i=13fi​(ξi,τi)⟨ξ1⟩s​⟨ξ2⟩s​⟨L1⟩b​⟨L2⟩b​⟨L3⟩1−b|≤C​∏i=13‖fi‖Lξ​τ2,∀{fi}1≤i≤3,\Bigg|\int\limits_{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=0}\int\limits_{\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}\tau_{i}=0}\frac{\xi_{3}\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{s}\prod\limits_{i=1}^{3}f_{i}(\xi_{i},\tau_{i})}{\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s}\langle L_{1}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{2}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-b}}\Bigg|\leq C\,\prod_{i=1}^{3}\|f_{i}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi\tau}},\quad\forall\,\{f_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq 3}, (5.2)

where

Li=τi−ϕαi​(ξi)=τi−αi​ξi3,1≤i≤3.L_{i}=\tau_{i}-\phi^{\alpha_{i}}(\xi_{i})=\tau_{i}-\alpha_{i}\xi_{i}^{3},\quad 1\leq i\leq 3.

In (5.2), the loss of the spatial derivative in the bilinear estimate (5.1) is reflected in the term ξ3​⟨ξ3⟩s⟨ξ1⟩s​⟨ξ2⟩s\frac{\xi_{3}\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{s}}{\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s}} and the gain of the time derivative is reflected in the term ⟨L1⟩b​⟨L2⟩b​⟨L3⟩1−b\langle L_{1}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{2}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-b}. Then how to compensate the loss of the spatial derivative from the gain of the time derivative is the key issue. Denote

K1=ξ3​⟨ξ3⟩s⟨ξ1⟩s​⟨ξ2⟩sandK2=⟨L1⟩b​⟨L2⟩b​⟨L3⟩1−b.K_{1}=\frac{\xi_{3}\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{s}}{\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s}}\quad\text{and}\quad K_{2}=\langle L_{1}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{2}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-b}.

Then the main idea is to control K1K_{1} by taking advantage of K2K_{2}. Since ∑i=13ξi=0\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=0, then ⟨ξ3⟩≤⟨ξ1⟩​⟨ξ2⟩\langle\xi_{3}\rangle\leq\langle\xi_{1}\rangle\langle\xi_{2}\rangle. As a result, K1K_{1} is a decreasing function in ss, which means the smaller ss is, the more likely the bilinear estimate will fail. So the question is how to find the smallest ss such that the bilinear estimate holds. Noticing that LiL_{i} contains the time variable τi\tau_{i}, so a single LiL_{i} can barely have any contributions. Since ∑i=13τi=0\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}\tau_{i}=0, then ∑i=13Li=−∑i=13αiξi3\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}L_{i}=-\sum\limits_{i=1}^{3}\alpha_{i}\xi_{i}^{3} is a function only in ξi\xi_{i}, 1≤i≤31\leq i\leq 3. Define

H⁡(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3):=∑i=13αi​ξi3.H(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3}):=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\alpha_{i}\xi_{i}^{3}.

Then it is obvious that K2≳|H|min⁡{b, 1−b}K_{2}\gtrsim|H|^{\min\{b,\,1-b\}}, which may be used to control K1K_{1}. Thus, H⁡(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)H(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3}) plays a fundamental role. In addition, HH measures to what extent the spatial frequencies ξ1\xi_{1}, ξ2\xi_{2} and ξ3\xi_{3} can resonate with each other. Because of this, HH is called the resonance function (see Page 856 in [47]). Unfortunately, |H||H| is not always large, the situation may become complicated near the region where HH vanishes. We shall call the zero set of HH to be the resonance set. Usually, the worst situation occurs near the resonance set and this trouble is called resonant interactions (see Page 856 in [47]).

In the following, we will investigate the resonance function and the resonance set in three typical situations (again {βi}i=13\{\beta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{3} are assumed to be zero for simplicity).

  • •

    In the classical case when α1=α2=α3\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}, the resonance function H0H_{0} is in a very simple form:

    H0​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=3​α1​ξ1​ξ2​ξ3.H_{0}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=3\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}\xi_{2}\xi_{3}.

    The resonance set consists of three hyperplanes: {ξi=0}\{\xi_{i}=0\}, i=1,2,3i=1,2,3.

  • •

    For the bilinear estimate of Type (D1), the resonance function H1H_{1} is

    H1​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=α1​ξ13+α1​ξ23+α2​ξ33.H_{1}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}^{3}+\alpha_{1}\xi_{2}^{3}+\alpha_{2}\xi_{3}^{3}.

    By writing ξ2=−(ξ1+ξ3)\xi_{2}=-(\xi_{1}+\xi_{3}),

    H1​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=ξ3​[(α2−α1)​ξ32−3​α1​ξ1​ξ3−3​α1​ξ12].H_{1}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\xi_{3}\Big[(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1})\xi_{3}^{2}-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}\xi_{3}-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}^{2}\Big].

    So {ξ3=0}\{\xi_{3}=0\} belongs to the resonance set. If ξ3≠0\xi_{3}\neq 0, then H1H_{1} can be rewritten as

    H1​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=−3​α1​ξ33​hr​(ξ1ξ3),H_{1}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{3}^{3}h_{r}\Big(\frac{\xi_{1}}{\xi_{3}}\Big),

    where r=α2α1r=\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{1}} and

    hr​(x):=x2+x+1−r3.h_{r}(x):=x^{2}+x+\frac{1-r}{3}.

    So the resonance set is determined by the roots of hrh_{r}.

  • •

    Similarly, for the bilinear estimate of Type (D2), the resonance function H2H_{2} is

    H2​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=α1​ξ13+α2​ξ23+α1​ξ33.H_{2}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}^{3}+\alpha_{2}\xi_{2}^{3}+\alpha_{1}\xi_{3}^{3}.

    By writing ξ3=−(ξ1+ξ2)\xi_{3}=-(\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}),

    H2​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=ξ2​[(α2−α1)​ξ22−3​α1​ξ1​ξ2−3​α1​ξ12].H_{2}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\xi_{2}\Big[(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1})\xi_{2}^{2}-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}\xi_{2}-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}^{2}\Big].

    So {ξ2=0}\{\xi_{2}=0\} belongs to the resonance set. If ξ2≠0\xi_{2}\neq 0, then H2H_{2} can be rewritten as

    H2​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=−3​α1​ξ23​hr​(ξ1ξ2).H_{2}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{2}^{3}h_{r}\Big(\frac{\xi_{1}}{\xi_{2}}\Big).

    Again the resonance set is determined by the roots of hrh_{r}.

Due to the above observations, the function hrh_{r} is crucial in determining the resonance set. The roots of hrh_{r} have three possibilities.

  • (1)

    If r<14r<\frac{1}{4}, then hrh_{r} does not have any real roots.

  • (2)

    If r=14r=\frac{1}{4}, then hrh_{r} has one real root −12-\frac{1}{2} of multiplicity 2.

  • (3)

    If r>14r>\frac{1}{4}, then hrh_{r} has two distinct real roots.

As we have seen, the structure of H1H_{1} is analogous to that of H2H_{2}. In addition, H0H_{0} is just a special case of H2H_{2} when r=1r=1. So in the following, we will just focus on H2H_{2} to discuss the effect of the resonance set on the threshold of ss.

  1. (i)

    r=1r=1. This agrees with the classical case and hrh_{r} has two roots x1​r=−1x_{1r}=-1 and x2​r=0x_{2r}=0. As we have seen that the resonance set of H0H_{0} consists of three hyperplanes {ξi=0}\{\xi_{i}=0\}, 1≤i≤31\leq i\leq 3. When s<0s<0, by writing ρ=−s\rho=-s, then ρ>0\rho>0 and

    K1∼⟨ξ1⟩ρ​⟨ξ2⟩ρ​|ξ3|1−ρ.K_{1}\sim\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{\rho}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{\rho}|\xi_{3}|^{1-\rho}.

    As a result, K1K_{1} is also small near the resonance set {ξi=0}\{\xi_{i}=0\}, 1≤i≤31\leq i\leq 3, which means the resonant interactions do not cause too much trouble. This is why the sharp index for the bilinear estimate of the divergence form can be as low as −34-\frac{3}{4} as shown in Lemma 3.2.

  2. (ii)

    r<14r<\frac{1}{4}. In this case, there exists a positive constant δr\delta_{r} such that hr​(x)≥δrh_{r}(x)\geq\delta_{r} for any x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R}. Consequently, the resonance set is only a single hyperplane {ξ2=0}\{\xi_{2}=0\}. Moreover, |ξ2|≪1|\xi_{2}|\ll 1 and |ξ1|∼|ξ3||\xi_{1}|\sim|\xi_{3}| near this hyperplane. As a result, |K1|∼|ξ3||K_{1}|\sim|\xi_{3}| does not depend on ss at all, which means the resonant interactions have no effect on ss in this case. So there is hope to obtain an even smaller threshold for ss. Actually, for Type (D2) with r<0r<0, ss can be as small as −1312-\frac{13}{12}.

  3. (iii)

    r>14r>\frac{1}{4} and r≠1r\neq 1. In this case, hrh_{r} has two distinct nonzero roots x1​rx_{1r} and x2​rx_{2r}. Therefore,

    H2​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=−3​α1​ξ23​(ξ1ξ2−x1​r)​(ξ1ξ2−x2​r).H_{2}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{2}^{3}\Big(\frac{\xi_{1}}{\xi_{2}}-x_{1r}\Big)\Big(\frac{\xi_{1}}{\xi_{2}}-x_{2r}\Big).

    The resonance set consists of three different hyperplanes: {ξ2=0}\{\xi_{2}=0\}, {ξ1=x1​rξ2}\{\xi_{1}=x_{1r}\xi_{2}\} and {ξ1=x2​rξ2}\{\xi_{1}=x_{2r}\xi_{2}\}. If s<0s<0, then near the hyperplane {ξ1=x1​rξ2}\{\xi_{1}=x_{1r}\xi_{2}\} or {ξ1=x2​rξ2}\{\xi_{1}=x_{2r}\xi_{2}\} with large ξ2\xi_{2}, the resonance function H2H_{2} is small while K1K_{1} is large. Thus, the bilinear estimate is likely to fail. Actually, the threshold for ss in this case is s≥0s\geq 0. This has already been pointed out by Oh[38].

  4. (iv)

    r=14r=\frac{1}{4}. In this case,

    H2​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=−3​α1​ξ23​(ξ1ξ2+12)2.H_{2}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{2}^{3}\Big(\frac{\xi_{1}}{\xi_{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\Big)^{2}.

    The resonance set consists of two hyperplanes {ξ2=0}\{\xi_{2}=0\} and {ξ1=−12ξ2}\{\xi_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}\xi_{2}\}. But the resonance interaction is significant near the hyperplane {ξ1=−12ξ2}\{\xi_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}\xi_{2}\} due to the square power. Consequently, the situation is expected to be worse. Actually, the bilinear estimate is valid only for s≥34s\geq\frac{3}{4}.

In addition to the resonant interactions, there is another trouble coming from coherent interactions (see [47]) when one has ∇ϕα1​(ξ1)=∇ϕα2​(ξ2)\nabla\phi^{\alpha_{1}}(\xi_{1})=\nabla\phi^{\alpha_{2}}(\xi_{2}), that is α1​ξ12=α2​ξ22\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}^{2}=\alpha_{2}\xi_{2}^{2}. Geometrically, coherent interactions occur when the surfaces τ1=ϕα1​(ξ1)\tau_{1}=\phi^{\alpha_{1}}(\xi_{1}) and τ2=ϕα2​(ξ2)\tau_{2}=\phi^{\alpha_{2}}(\xi_{2}) fail to be transverse. For example, when r<14r<\frac{1}{4}, as we just discussed above, the resonance set of H2H_{2} is a sinlge hyperplane: {ξ2=0}\{\xi_{2}=0\} no matter r<0r<0 or 0<r<140<r<\frac{1}{4}. However, the critical indexes for ss are different in these two cases.

  • •

    If r<0r<0, then α1​ξ12\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}^{2} will not match α2​ξ22\alpha_{2}\xi_{2}^{2} regardless of the values of ξ1\xi_{1} and ξ2\xi_{2}. So the coherent interactions do not occur in this case and the sharp index for ss is −1312-\frac{13}{12}.

  • •

    If r>0r>0, then α1​ξ12=α2​ξ22\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}^{2}=\alpha_{2}\xi_{2}^{2} when ξ1=±r​ξ2\xi_{1}=\pm\sqrt{r}\xi_{2}. So the coherent interactions occur along the hyperplanes {ξ1=±rξ2}\{\xi_{1}=\pm\sqrt{r}\xi_{2}\}. It turns out that the critical index for this case is −34-\frac{3}{4}.

The above arguments revealed the difficulties for the bilinear estimate of the divergence form. These difficulties play the similar role in the nondivergence case. But the nondivergence form can bring additional trouble. Let us compare (D2) and (ND1) with r=1r=1 and βi=0​(i=1,2)\beta_{i}=0\,(i=1,2). In this case, the resonance functions for (D2) and (ND1) are the same, both of them are equal to H0H_{0}. However, the terms K1K_{1} and K~1\widetilde{K}_{1} coming from the loss of the spatial derivative for (D1) and (ND1) are different. More precisely,

K1=ξ3​⟨ξ3⟩s⟨ξ1⟩s​⟨ξ2⟩sandK~1=ξ1​⟨ξ3⟩s⟨ξ1⟩s​⟨ξ2⟩s.K_{1}=\frac{\xi_{3}\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{s}}{\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s}}\quad\text{and}\quad\widetilde{K}_{1}=\frac{\xi_{1}\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{s}}{\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s}}.

Consider s=−34+s=-\frac{3}{4}+, then

|K1|∼|ξ3|​⟨ξ1⟩34−​⟨ξ2⟩34−⟨ξ3⟩34−and|K~1|∼|ξ1|​⟨ξ1⟩34−​⟨ξ2⟩34−⟨ξ3⟩34−.|K_{1}|\sim\frac{|\xi_{3}|\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{\frac{3}{4}-}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{\frac{3}{4}-}}{\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{\frac{3}{4}-}}\quad\text{and}\quad|\widetilde{K}_{1}|\sim\frac{|\xi_{1}|\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{\frac{3}{4}-}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{\frac{3}{4}-}}{\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{\frac{3}{4}-}}.

Previously, the worst region for (D2) is when |ξ1|∼|ξ2|≫|ξ3||\xi_{1}|\sim|\xi_{2}|\gg|\xi_{3}| and this forces ss to be greater than −3/4-3/4. But in this region, it is easily seen that K~1\widetilde{K}_{1} is even much larger than K1K_{1}. So there is no hope to control K~1\widetilde{K}_{1} as well when ss is near −3/4-3/4. Actually, it will be shown that the critical index for (ND1) is 0.

In summary, there are three main troubles in establishing the bilinear estimates (3.4)-(3.7).

  • (T1)

    : resonant interactions;

  • (T2)

    : coherent interaction;

  • (T3)

    : the nondivergence form in the region |ξ1|∼|ξ2|≫|ξ3||\xi_{1}|\sim|\xi_{2}|\gg|\xi_{3}|.

Generally speaking, (T1) is the most significant trouble and (T2) and (T3) are of the same level of influence. In most cases, these troubles do not occur at the same place, then the strategy is simply to divide the region suitably and deal with one trouble in each region. However, if more than one trouble occur at the same place, then the situation is expected to be worse. In the following, we provide Table 22 to present the main trouble and the critical indexes for ss in each case for the bilinear estimates (3.4)-(3.7). The sign “+” indicates the situation when two troubles occur at the same place.

5.2 Auxiliary lemmas

Lemma 5.1.

Let ρ1>1\rho_{1}>1 and 0≤ρ2≤ρ10\leq\rho_{2}\leq\rho_{1} be given. There exists a constant C=C⁡(ρ1,ρ2)C=C(\rho_{1},\rho_{2}) such that for any α,β∈ℝ\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R},

∫−∞∞d​x⟨x−α⟩ρ1​⟨−x−β⟩ρ2≤C⟨α+β⟩ρ2.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\langle x-\alpha\rangle^{\rho_{1}}\langle-x-\beta\rangle^{\rho_{2}}}\leq\frac{C}{\langle\alpha+\beta\rangle^{\rho_{2}}}. (5.3)

The proof for this lemma is standard and therefore omitted, we just want to remark that ⟨α+β⟩=⟨(x−α)+(−x−β)⟩\langle\alpha+\beta\rangle=\langle(x-\alpha)+(-x-\beta)\rangle, this observation will be used in the estimate (5.34).

Lemma 5.2.

If ρ>12\rho>\frac{1}{2}, then there exists C=C⁡(ρ)C=C(\rho) such that for any σi∈ℝ, 0≤i≤2\sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R},\,0\leq i\leq 2, with σ2≠0\sigma_{2}\neq 0,

∫−∞∞d​x⟨σ2​x2+σ1​x+σ0⟩ρ≤C|σ2|1/2.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\langle\sigma_{2}x^{2}+\sigma_{1}x+\sigma_{0}\rangle^{\rho}}\leq\frac{C}{|\sigma_{2}|^{1/2}}. (5.4)

Similarly, if ρ>13\rho>\frac{1}{3}, then there exists C=C⁡(ρ)C=C(\rho) such that for any σi∈ℝ, 0≤i≤3\sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R},\,0\leq i\leq 3, with σ3≠0\sigma_{3}\neq 0,

∫−∞∞d​x⟨σ3​x3+σ2​x2+σ1​x+σ0⟩ρ≤C|σ3|1/3.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\langle\sigma_{3}x^{3}+\sigma_{2}x^{2}+\sigma_{1}x+\sigma_{0}\rangle^{\rho}}\leq\frac{C}{|\sigma_{3}|^{1/3}}. (5.5)
Proof.

We refer the reader to the proof of Lemma 2.5 in [3] where (5.5) was proved. The similar argument can also be applied to obtain (5.4). ∎

If the power ρ\rho in Lemma 5.2 is greater than 1, then stronger conclusions hold.

Lemma 5.3.

Let ρ>1\rho>1 be given. There exists a constant C=C⁡(ρ)C=C(\rho) such that for any σi∈ℝ, 0≤i≤2\sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R},\,0\leq i\leq 2, with σ2≠0\sigma_{2}\neq 0,

∫−∞∞d​x⟨σ2​x2+σ1​x+σ0⟩ρ≤C​|σ2|−12​⟨σ0−σ124​σ2⟩−12.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\langle\sigma_{2}x^{2}+\sigma_{1}x+\sigma_{0}\rangle^{\rho}}\leq C\,|\sigma_{2}|^{-\frac{1}{2}}\Big\langle\sigma_{0}-\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{4\sigma_{2}}\Big\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}}. (5.6)

It suffices to consider the case when σ2>0\sigma_{2}>0. By rewriting

σ2​x2+σ1​x+σ0=σ2​(x+σ12​σ2)2+σ0−σ124​σ2\sigma_{2}x^{2}+\sigma_{1}x+\sigma_{0}=\sigma_{2}\Big(x+\frac{\sigma_{1}}{2\sigma_{2}}\Big)^{2}+\sigma_{0}-\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{4\sigma_{2}}

and doing a change of variable y=σ2​(x+σ12​σ2)y=\sqrt{\sigma_{2}}\big(x+\frac{\sigma_{1}}{2\sigma_{2}}\big), it reduces to show for any α∈ℝ\alpha\in\mathbb{R},

∫−∞∞d​y⟨y2+α⟩ρ≤C​⟨α⟩−12,\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dy}{\langle y^{2}+\alpha\rangle^{\rho}}\leq C\langle\alpha\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}},

for which, the verification is straightforward and left to the readers. ∎

Lemma 5.4.

Let ρ>1\rho>1 be given. There exists a constant C=C⁡(ρ)C=C(\rho) such that for any σi∈ℝ, 0≤i≤2\sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R},\,0\leq i\leq 2,

∫−∞∞d​x⟨x3+σ2​x2+σ1​x+σ0⟩ρ≤C​⟨3​σ1−σ22⟩−14.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\langle x^{3}+\sigma_{2}x^{2}+\sigma_{1}x+\sigma_{0}\rangle^{\rho}}\leq C\big\langle 3\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2}^{2}\big\rangle^{-\frac{1}{4}}. (5.7)
Proof.

By the change of variable y=x+σ23y=x+\frac{\sigma_{2}}{3},

∫−∞∞d​x⟨x3+σ2​x2+σ1​x+σ0⟩ρ=∫−∞∞d​y⟨y3+b1​y+b0⟩ρ,\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\langle x^{3}+\sigma_{2}x^{2}+\sigma_{1}x+\sigma_{0}\rangle^{\rho}}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dy}{\langle y^{3}+b_{1}y+b_{0}\rangle^{\rho}},

where

b1=σ1−13​σ22,b0=227​σ23−13​σ1​σ2+σ0.b_{1}=\sigma_{1}-\frac{1}{3}\sigma_{2}^{2},\quad b_{0}=\frac{2}{27}\sigma_{2}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}+\sigma_{0}.

Thus, (5.7) reduces to justify

∫−∞∞d​y⟨y3+b1​y+b0⟩ρ≤C​⟨b1⟩−14\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dy}{\langle y^{3}+b_{1}y+b_{0}\rangle^{\rho}}\leq C\langle b_{1}\rangle^{-\frac{1}{4}} (5.8)

for some constant CC which only depends on ρ\rho. If |b1|≲1|b_{1}|\lesssim 1, then (5.8) follows from (5.5) in Lemma 5.2. If |b1|≫1|b_{1}|\gg 1, we define g⁡(y)=y3+b1​y+b0g(y)=y^{3}+b_{1}y+b_{0} and find g′​(y)=3​y2+b1g^{\prime}(y)=3y^{2}+b_{1}. If |g′​(y)|≥|b1|1/4|g^{\prime}(y)|\geq|b_{1}|^{1/4}, then

∫d​y⟨g⁡(y)⟩ρ≤∫1|b1|1/4​|g′​(y)|⟨g⁡(y)⟩ρ​𝑑y≤C​⟨b1⟩−14.\int\frac{dy}{\langle g(y)\rangle^{\rho}}\leq\int\frac{1}{|b_{1}|^{1/4}}\frac{|g^{\prime}(y)|}{\langle g(y)\rangle^{\rho}}\,dy\leq C\langle b_{1}\rangle^{-\frac{1}{4}}.

If |g′​(y)|≤|b1|1/4|g^{\prime}(y)|\leq|b_{1}|^{1/4}, then the measure of the set of these yy values is at most O⁡(|b1|−14)O\big(|b_{1}|^{-\frac{1}{4}}\big), so the integral of ⟨g⁡(y)⟩−ρ\langle g(y)\rangle^{-\rho} on this set is also bounded by C⟨b1⟩−1/4C\langle b_{1}\rangle^{-1/4}. ∎

For the proof of the bilinear estimate, it is usually beneficial to transfer it to an estimate of some weighted convolution of L2L^{2} functions as pointed out in [47, 11]. The next lemma is one of such an example for the general bilinear estimate whose proof is standard by using duality and Plancherel theorem. For the convenience of notation, we denote ξ→=(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)\vec{\xi}=(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3}) and τ→=(τ1,τ2,τ3)\vec{\tau}=(\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\tau_{3}) to be the vectors in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and define

A:={(ξ→,τ→)∈ℝ6:∑i=13ξi=∑i=13τi=0}.A:=\Big\{(\vec{\xi},\vec{\tau})\in\mathbb{R}^{6}:\sum_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\tau_{i}=0\Big\}. (5.9)
Lemma 5.5.

Given ss, bb and (αi,βi)​1≤i≤3(\alpha_{i},\beta_{i})1\leq i\leq 3, the bilinear estimate

‖∂x(w1​w2)‖Xs,b−1α3,β3≤C​‖w1‖Xs,bα1,β1​‖w2‖Xs,bα2,β2,∀{wi}i=1,2,\|\partial_{x}(w_{1}w_{2})\|_{X^{\alpha_{3},\beta_{3}}_{s,b-1}}\leq C\,\|w_{1}\|_{X^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}_{s,b}}\,\|w_{2}\|_{X^{\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}}_{s,b}},\quad\forall\,\{w_{i}\}_{i=1,2},

is equivalent to

where

Li=τi−ϕαi,βi(ξi),i=1,2,3.L_{i}=\tau_{i}-\phi^{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}}(\xi_{i}),\quad i=1,2,3. (5.11)

5.3 Resonance functions and the characteristic quadratic function

Based on the discussion in Section 5.1, the resonance function plays an essential role in establishing bilinear estimates. Now we follow [47] to give a formal definition to this function in the most general form.

Definition 5.6 ([47]).

Let ((a1,β1),(α2,β2),(α3,β3))\big((a_{1},\beta_{1}),(\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}),(\alpha_{3},\beta_{3})\big) be a triple in (ℝ∗×ℝ)3(\mathbb{R}^{*}\times\mathbb{R})^{3}. Define the resonance function HH associated to this triple by

H⁡(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=∑i=13ϕαi,βi​(ξi),∀∑i=13ξi=0.H(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\phi^{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}}(\xi_{i}),\quad\forall\,\sum_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=0. (5.12)

The resonance set of HH is defined to be the zero set of HH, that is

{(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)∈ℝ3:∑i=13ξi=0,H(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=0}.\Big\{(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}:\sum_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=0,\,H(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=0\Big\}. (5.13)

In particular, we introduce the notations of H0H_{0}, H1H_{1} and H2H_{2}.

  • (1)

    The resonance function associated to the triple ((a1,β1),(α1,β1),(α1,β1))\big((a_{1},\beta_{1}),(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}),(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1})\big) is denoted as H0H_{0}:

    H0​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=∑i=13ϕα1,β1​(ξi),∀∑i=13ξi=0.H_{0}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}(\xi_{i}),\quad\forall\,\sum_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=0. (5.14)

    This applies to the classical case (3.3) or the case r=1r=1 in Table 20. By direct calculation,

    H0​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=3​α1​ξ1​ξ2​ξ3.H_{0}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=3\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}\xi_{2}\xi_{3}.
  • (2)

    The resonance function associated to the triple ((a1,β1),(α1,β1),(α2,β2))\big((a_{1},\beta_{1}),(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}),(\alpha_{2},\beta_{2})\big) is denoted as H1H_{1}:

    H1​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=ϕα1,β1​(ξ1)+ϕα1,β1​(ξ2)+ϕα2,β2​(ξ3),∀∑i=13ξi=0.H_{1}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}(\xi_{1})+\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}(\xi_{2})+\phi^{\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}}(\xi_{3}),\quad\forall\,\sum_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=0. (5.15)

    This applies to the bilinear estimate of Type (D1). By direct calculation and writing ξ2=−(ξ1+ξ3)\xi_{2}=-(\xi_{1}+\xi_{3}),

    H1​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=ξ3​[(α2−α1)​ξ32−3​α1​ξ1​ξ3−3​α1​ξ12]+(β1−β2)​ξ3.H_{1}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\xi_{3}\Big[(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1})\xi_{3}^{2}-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}\xi_{3}-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{1}^{2}\Big]+(\beta_{1}-\beta_{2})\xi_{3}. (5.16)

    If ξ3=0\xi_{3}=0, then H1=0H_{1}=0. If ξ3≠0\xi_{3}\neq 0, then H1H_{1} can be rewritten as

    H1​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=−3​α1​ξ33​hr​(ξ1ξ3)+(β1−β2)​ξ3,H_{1}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=-3\alpha_{1}\xi_{3}^{3}h_{r}\Big(\frac{\xi_{1}}{\xi_{3}}\Big)+(\beta_{1}-\beta_{2})\xi_{3}, (5.17)

    where r=α2α1r=\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{1}} and

    hr​(x):=x2+x+1−r3.h_{r}(x):=x^{2}+x+\frac{1-r}{3}. (5.18)
  • (3)

    The resonance function H2H_{2} associated to the triple ((a1,β1),(α2,β2),(α1,β1))\big((a_{1},\beta_{1}),(\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}),(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1})\big) is denoted as H2H_{2}:

    H2​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)=ϕα1,β1​(ξ1)+ϕα2,β2​(ξ2)+ϕα1,β1​(ξ3),∀∑i=13ξi=0.H_{2}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})=\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}(\xi_{1})+\phi^{\alpha_{2},\beta_{2}}(\xi_{2})+\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}}(\xi_{3}),\quad\forall\,\sum_{i=1}^{3}\xi_{i}=0. (5.19)

According to the above computation, the quadratic function hrh_{r} is essential to determine the behavior of H1H_{1} and H2H_{2}, thus, it is a characterization of the coupled KdV-KdV systems.

Definition 5.7.

The quadratic function hrh_{r} in (5.18) is called the characteristic quadratic function associated to the coupled KdV-KdV systems (1.2).

For the convenience of the proof, we introduce some notations below. For any r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}, we define hrh_{r} as in (5.18) and define pr:ℝ→ℝp_{r}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} by

5.5 Proof of Theorem 3.5

First, we want to point out several cases in Table 20 which have been known or can be proved similarly.

In all of the above results, it is assumed that β1=β2=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0. But as we have seen from the proof of Theorem 3.3, even if β1\beta_{1} or β2\beta_{2} is not equal to 00, they will not affect the conclusion as long as |β2−β1||\beta_{2}-\beta_{1}| is small.

For the rest cases in Table 20, we will only provide proofs for the following typical ones.

  1. (1)

    Among the cases when r<0r<0 or 0<r<140<r<\frac{1}{4}, we will only prove Type (ND1) with 0<r<140<r<\frac{1}{4}, see Section 5.5.1. There are two reasons. Firstly, the cases when 0<r<140<r<\frac{1}{4} is generally more difficult than the cases when r<0r<0. Secondly, the non-divergence cases is more challenging than the divergence cases.

  3. (3)

    satisfies B1+B3⊆−B2B_{1}+B_{3}\subseteq-B_{2}. Moreover, |B1|∼|B3|∼|B2|∼N−12|B_{1}|\sim|B_{3}|\sim|B_{2}|\sim N^{-\frac{1}{2}}. Choosing fi=𝟙Bif_{i}=\mathbbm{1}_{B_{i}} (1≤i≤31\leq i\leq 3) in (6.2) yields

    C​∏i=13|Bi|12≥∫Aξ3​⟨ξ3⟩s​∏i=13𝟙Bi​(ξi,τi)⟨ξ1⟩s​⟨ξ2⟩s​⟨L1⟩b​⟨L2⟩b​⟨L3⟩1−b.C\,\prod_{i=1}^{3}|B_{i}|^{\frac{1}{2}}\geq\int\limits_{A}\frac{\xi_{3}\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{s}\prod\limits_{i=1}^{3}\mathbbm{1}_{B_{i}}(\xi_{i},\tau_{i})}{\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s}\langle L_{1}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{2}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-b}}. (6.9)

    As for any (ξi,τi)∈Bi(\xi_{i},\tau_{i})\in B_{i}, 1≤i≤31\leq i\leq 3,

    |L1|≤1,|L3|≤1,|H2​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)|∼N3,|L_{1}|\leq 1,\quad|L_{3}|\leq 1,\quad|H_{2}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})|\sim N^{3},

    we have |L2|=|H2+L1+L3|∼N3|L_{2}|=|H_{2}+L_{1}+L_{3}|\sim N^{3}. It then follows from (6.9) and Lemma 6.1 that

    N−34≳N1+sN2​s​N3​b​∫A∏i=13𝟙Bi​(ξi,τi)=N1+s|B1∥B3|N2​s​N3​b∼1Ns​N3​b,N^{-\frac{3}{4}}\gtrsim\frac{N^{1+s}}{N^{2s}N^{3b}}\int\limits_{A}\prod_{i=1}^{3}\mathbbm{1}_{B_{i}}(\xi_{i},\tau_{i})=\frac{N^{1+s}|B_{1}\|B_{3}|}{N^{2s}N^{3b}}\sim\frac{1}{N^{s}N^{3b}},

    which implies (6.8).

Combining (6.5) and (6.8) together yields s≥−1312s\geq-\frac{13}{12}, which contradicts to the assumption s<−1312s<-\frac{13}{12}.

Proof of Case (2).

If −1312≤s≤−1-\frac{13}{12}\leq s\leq-1, the same arguments as in the proofs of Claim A and Claim B show that (6.5) and (6.8) are necessary conditions on bb if the bilinear estimate (3.5) holds.

Proof of Case (3).

Let −1<s<−34-1<s<-\frac{3}{4}. The same argument as in the proof of Claim B shows b≥14−s3b\geq\frac{1}{4}-\frac{s}{3}. To obtain the desired upper bound for bb, let

B1\displaystyle B_{1} :={(ξ1,τ1):N−1≤ξ1≤N,|τ1−ϕα1,β(ξ1)|≤1},\displaystyle:=\big\{(\xi_{1},\tau_{1}):N-1\leq\xi_{1}\leq N,\quad\big|\tau_{1}-\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta}(\xi_{1})\big|\leq 1\big\},
B2\displaystyle B_{2} :={(ξ2,τ2):N−1≤ξ2≤N,|τ2−ϕα2,β(ξ2)|≤1}.\displaystyle:=\big\{(\xi_{2},\tau_{2}):N-1\leq\xi_{2}\leq N,\quad\big|\tau_{2}-\phi^{\alpha_{2},\beta}(\xi_{2})\big|\leq 1\big\}.

Then similar to the procedure in the proof of Claim A in Case (1), there exists a suitably large constant C3C_{3} such that the set

B3:={(ξ3,τ3):−2N≤ξ3≤−2N+2,|τ3+(α1+α2)N3|≤C3N2}B_{3}:=\{(\xi_{3},\tau_{3}):-2N\leq\xi_{3}\leq-2N+2,\quad|\tau_{3}+(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})N^{3}|\leq C_{3}N^{2}\}

has the property B1+B2⊆−B3B_{1}+B_{2}\subseteq-B_{3}. In addition, |B1|=|B2|=2|B_{1}|=|B_{2}|=2 and |B3|∼N2|B_{3}|\sim N^{2}. Choosing fi=−𝟙Bif_{i}=-\mathbbm{1}_{B_{i}} (1≤i≤31\leq i\leq 3) in (6.2) yields

C​∏i=13|Bi|12≥∫A−ξ3⟨ξ3⟩s∏i=13𝟙Bi(ξi,τi)⟨ξ1⟩s​⟨ξ2⟩s​⟨L1⟩b​⟨L2⟩b​⟨L3⟩1−b.C\,\prod_{i=1}^{3}|B_{i}|^{\frac{1}{2}}\geq\int\limits_{A}\frac{-\xi_{3}\langle\xi_{3}\rangle^{s}\prod\limits_{i=1}^{3}\mathbbm{1}_{B_{i}}(\xi_{i},\tau_{i})}{\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s}\langle L_{1}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{2}\rangle^{b}\langle L_{3}\rangle^{1-b}}. (6.10)

For any (ξi,τi)∈Bi(\xi_{i},\tau_{i})\in B_{i}, 1≤i≤31\leq i\leq 3,

|L1|≤1,|L2|≤1,|H2​(ξ1,ξ2,ξ3)|∼N3,|L3|∼N3.|L_{1}|\leq 1,\quad|L_{2}|\leq 1,\quad|H_{2}(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3})|\sim N^{3},\quad|L_{3}|\sim N^{3}.

It then follows from (6.10) and Lemma 6.1 that b≤1+s3b\leq 1+\frac{s}{3}.

6.2 Proof of Theorem 3.6

First, we want to point out several cases in Table 21 which have been known or can be proved similarly. When r=1r=1, the bilinear estimates of Type (D1) and (D2) have been known to fail if s<−34s<-\frac{3}{4}, see [29]. When r>14r>\frac{1}{4} but r≠1r\neq 1, the bilinear estimates of Type (D1) and (D2) do not hold for s<0s<0, see [38]. The situations for Type (ND1) and (ND2) can be treated similarly.

For the rest cases in Table 21, we will only prove the failure of the bilinear estimates in the following five cases since other cases are similar. Case (1): Type (D1) with r<0r<0 and s<−34s<-\frac{3}{4}. Case (2): Type (D2) with 0<r<140<r<\frac{1}{4} and s<−34s<-\frac{3}{4}. Case (3): Type (ND1) with r<0r<0 and s<−34s<-\frac{3}{4}. Case (4): Type (ND1) with r=14r=\frac{1}{4} and s<34s<\frac{3}{4}. Case (5): Type (ND1) with r=1r=1 and s<0s<0.

Moreover, the general strategy for all the above cases is very similar to that in the proof of Theorem 3.4 as shown above. The key ingredient is to construct suitable {Bi}i=13\{B_{i}\}_{i=1}^{3}. So in the following, we will only write out the sets {Bi}i=13\{B_{i}\}_{i=1}^{3} that works for the argument, but omit the detailed computations which can be easily carried out.

Proof of Case (1). For any large number N>0N>0, define

B1\displaystyle B_{1} ={(ξ1,τ1):N−1≤ξ1≤N,12N≤|τ1−ϕα1,β(ξ1)|≤N},\displaystyle=\big\{(\xi_{1},\tau_{1}):N-1\leq\xi_{1}\leq N,\quad\frac{1}{2}N\leq\big|\tau_{1}-\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta}(\xi_{1})\big|\leq N\big\},
B2\displaystyle B_{2} ={(ξ2,τ2):−N−2≤ξ2≤−N−1,12N≤|τ2−ϕα1,β(ξ2)|≤N}.\displaystyle=\big\{(\xi_{2},\tau_{2}):-N-2\leq\xi_{2}\leq-N-1,\quad\frac{1}{2}N\leq\big|\tau_{2}-\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta}(\xi_{2})\big|\leq N\big\}.

Then we choose a suitably large constant C1C_{1} such that the set

B3:={(ξ3,τ3):1≤ξ3≤3,|τ3−3α1N2ξ3|≤C1N}B_{3}:=\{(\xi_{3},\tau_{3}):1\leq\xi_{3}\leq 3,\quad|\tau_{3}-3\alpha_{1}N^{2}\xi_{3}|\leq C_{1}N\}

satisfies B1+B2⊆−B3B_{1}+B_{2}\subseteq-B_{3}.

Proof of Case (2). For large number N>0N>0, define

B1\displaystyle B_{1} :={(ξ1,τ1):N−N−12≤ξ1≤N,|τ1−ϕα1,β(ξ1)|≤1},\displaystyle:=\big\{(\xi_{1},\tau_{1}):N-N^{-\frac{1}{2}}\leq\xi_{1}\leq N,\quad\big|\tau_{1}-\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta}(\xi_{1})\big|\leq 1\big\},
B2\displaystyle B_{2} :={(ξ2,τ2):r−12N−N−12≤ξ2≤r−12N,|τ2−ϕα2,β(ξ2)|≤1}.\displaystyle:=\big\{(\xi_{2},\tau_{2}):r^{-\frac{1}{2}}N-N^{-\frac{1}{2}}\leq\xi_{2}\leq r^{-\frac{1}{2}}N,\quad\big|\tau_{2}-\phi^{\alpha_{2},\beta}(\xi_{2})\big|\leq 1\big\}.

Then we choose a suitably large constant C1C_{1} such that the set

satisfies B1+B2⊆−B3B_{1}+B_{2}\subseteq-B_{3}.

Proof of Case (3). For large number N>0N>0, define

B1\displaystyle B_{1} :={(ξ1,τ1):N−N−12≤ξ1≤N,12N32≤|τ1−ϕα1,β(ξ1)|≤N32},\displaystyle:=\big\{(\xi_{1},\tau_{1}):N-N^{-\frac{1}{2}}\leq\xi_{1}\leq N,\quad\frac{1}{2}N^{\frac{3}{2}}\leq\big|\tau_{1}-\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta}(\xi_{1})\big|\leq N^{\frac{3}{2}}\big\},

satisfies B1+B2⊆−B3B_{1}+B_{2}\subseteq-B_{3}.

Proof of Case (4). For large N>0N>0, define

B1\displaystyle B_{1} ={(ξ1,τ1):N−N−12≤ξ1≤N,|τ1−ϕα1,β(ξ1)|≤1},\displaystyle=\big\{(\xi_{1},\tau_{1}):N-N^{-\frac{1}{2}}\leq\xi_{1}\leq N,\quad\big|\tau_{1}-\phi^{\alpha_{1},\beta}(\xi_{1})\big|\leq 1\big\},
